label: GPT-6.1 Sol
output:
Dear Nana,

I wish I were sitting in the kitchen with you tonight. I wish I could have a cup of tea with you and Aunt Denise, and stay up too late talking, and be there tomorrow to carry boxes and get in everybody’s way. Being in Toronto while you’re getting ready to leave Kathleen Street feels wrong, even though I know you’d tell me not to be silly.

I’m primary on call all week, and I couldn’t find anyone to swap with me. I know you understand. But I’m still sorry I can’t be there. I won’t spend this whole letter apologizing, because then you’ll have to spend your last evening in the kitchen reassuring me, and that hardly seems fair. I just want you to know I wanted to be there. Very much.

I’ve been trying to write this all week. I keep starting, getting a few lines down, and closing the laptop. For someone whose job is dealing with things breaking, I have not been especially useful when faced with my own feelings.

You’ll probably want to know whether anything broke today. If it did, someone is dealing with it. For once, you have my permission not to worry about the internet.

I keep thinking about all the summers I spent at your house, and how much of them happened in that kitchen. At the time, I thought the important thing was that you let me stay up to watch the Expos or the Jays on the little television, as long as I dried the dishes. This seemed like an excellent arrangement to me. I got baseball and a later bedtime, and you got someone to stand beside you with a tea towel.

Looking back, I think you may have got more out of that deal than I realized. Although I also suspect you had to put away quite a few dishes that weren’t completely dry.

I loved being there with you. I didn’t have to have anything interesting to say. I could just stand there, drying a plate, watching the game, being allowed to stay up. Those evenings felt ordinary because you made them feel ordinary. I didn’t know then that I’d still be thinking about them at thirty-four.

And I think about the back steps. You’d be out there at six in the morning with your tea, and I’d come out to sit with you. You never talked until the cup was finished. I learned that rule fairly quickly. I liked it, actually. There wasn’t much I needed to say at six in the morning either.

I miss being able to come outside and find you there.

There’s so much I associate with that house that it’s hard to separate one memory from another. Fifty-one years is a long time. You raised half the family in that kitchen. I don’t know how you managed to feed everybody and listen to everybody and still have enough patience left to teach a seven-year-old to play crib.

Though perhaps patience isn’t the right word for what happened at the crib board. You taught me the rules, certainly. You did not believe that being seven entitled me to any special treatment.

I’m glad you never let me win. I’m allowed to say that now, from a safe distance, as an adult. At the time I probably would have appreciated a little less commitment to fairness.

But the first time I skunked you, when I was fifteen, you made me a whole pan of butter tarts. You have to admit that was a dangerous precedent. You spent years teaching me to be a gracious loser, then made winning against you the most rewarding experience of my young life.

I still remember how pleased I was. About the game, obviously, but also about the butter tarts, and about you being pleased with me even though I’d beaten you.

That’s why I asked for the crib board. I want to keep playing on the board you taught me on. I like thinking that years from now I’ll still be counting my hand on it, checking twice because I can practically hear you waiting for me to miss something.

Denise is taking the cuckoo clock and the cedar chest, and I’m glad those things are staying in the family too. There are familiar pieces of the house going with different people who love you. We’ll all be looking after them.

I know this move means leaving more than the building. There are fifty-one years of your life there, and so much of your life with Grandpa Walt. I’ve been thinking about him too. I wish he could be here with us.

I won’t pretend that leaving is a small thing, or that you have to feel only one way about it. You can be excited about Elmwood Terrace and still have a hard evening tonight. You can miss the house after you’ve moved. You don’t have to make us feel better about any of that.

But I also don’t want to talk as though all the good things are behind you, because they aren’t. You’ve chosen a new place to live, and I’m excited to see it.

I’m proud of you, Nana. You decided to do this yourself. You looked at what you wanted and picked Elmwood Terrace. Nobody made the choice for you. I know there must have been a lot to think about, and a lot to sort through, and probably a few days when you’d had quite enough of sorting through it. I really admire you for doing it.

I want to see your room on the second floor, and the big maple outside your window. The parking lot may not have been the main selling point, but you’ll be well placed to keep track of who’s coming and going.

And I hear there’s a crib league.

I’m very happy for you, although I feel someone ought to warn them. They may think they’re welcoming a nice eighty-eight-year-old lady who plays cards with her church friends on Tuesdays. They should know that being new will not stop you from skunking them.

It makes me happy to imagine you getting to know people there. I want to hear who you’ve met and how the games are going and what you think of the place once you’re properly in. You’ll still have your Tuesday church ladies, and now there’ll be more people to play with. That sounds like a fairly good arrangement.

There’s something else I wanted to say while Denise has to do the reading and you can’t interrupt me to wave it away.

Thank you for looking after me so well, for so long.

I still think about the card you sent when I got the job in Toronto, with twenty dollars taped inside and “for pizza, you look thin on the computer.” I loved that. I had a proper job and was supposed to be a grown-up, and you were still making sure I had something to eat.

You’ve never needed a particularly convincing reason to take care of me. A slightly unflattering video call was enough.

And last Christmas, when my pager went off during dinner and you asked if the internet was broken again, and whether I’d fixed it, you made an interruption I was annoyed about into something I could laugh at. Now every time you ask, “Did anything break?” I’m glad you remember to ask about my work, even if my explanation of it has apparently left you thinking Toronto depends entirely on me turning the internet back on.

I love that you ask. I love knowing you want to hear how my day went.

The house meant so much to me because I got to spend that time with you there. I’m going to miss it. I’ll miss the kitchen and the back steps, and knowing exactly where I was coming when I said I was coming to see Nana. I’m sure the first visit somewhere else will feel strange.

But I’m still coming to see Nana. We’ll have plenty to talk about, and you’ll still want to know whether I’ve eaten. I’ll probably tell you something about work that makes no sense, and then we can get the cards out.

December 5. That’s when I’m coming up, once this rotation is done. We’ll have our first game at the new place that weekend. We can sit by the window with the maple outside, and you can tell me everything.

I love you very much. I wish I could give you a hug tonight. Denise, please do that part for me.

I’ll see you on December 5, Nana. Have the crib board ready.

And if I skunk you, I assume the butter tart arrangement still stands.

All my love,

Your grandkid
